stories.headline: Riley's homer rallies Braves past Phillies in wild-card opener
stories.summary: Austin Riley hit a three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran in the eighth inning, and the Braves rallied past the Phillies 5-3 on Tuesday in the opener their National League Wild Card Series.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- Austin Riley hit a three-run homer off All-Star closer Jhoan Duran in the eighth inning and the Atlanta Braves rallied past the Philadelphia Phillies 5-3 on Tuesday in the opener of a best-of-three National League Wild Card Series.

Duran (0-1), who allowed just two homers in 61 regular-season games, gave up a single to Michael Harris II before hitting Ozzie Albies with a pitch. Riley drove the go-ahead blast over the wall in right-center field. Harris had three hits.

The Braves can clinch the series on Wednesday and end the Phillies' history of postseason success in the NL East rivalry. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.

Braves ace Chris Sale dueled for much of the game against left-hander Jesus Luzardo, who was sharp after missing the last couple weeks of the regular season with left shoulder inflammation. Luzardo was expected to make an abbreviated start, but he pitched one-run ball over five innings with 77 pitches.

Atlanta pounced when Philadelphia went to the bullpen - a common theme for the Phillies as they slumped into the postseason. Their relievers had a 5.79 ERA in September, worst in the majors.

Albies hit a tiebreaking triple off Alex McFarlane in the sixth for a 2-1 lead. Center fielder Derek Hill had an opportunity to make a leaping catch of Albies' drive at the wall, but he appeared to jump too high. The ball hit Hill's wrist below his glove.

J.T. Realmuto put Philadelphia ahead 3-2 with a two-run triple in the seventh inning - right fielder Ronald Acuna Jr. bobbled the ball near the wall, but he wasn't charged with an error.

Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly handed the ball over to Duran in the seventh, perhaps hoping the 28-year-old had three innings in him to close things out. Duran made just one multi-inning appearance this season.

Sale gave up three runs as he faded in the seventh in his effort to deliver as the ace of Atlanta's depleted rotation.

Sale hit Bryan De La Cruz with a pitch with one out in the seventh before giving up a single to Bryson Stott. Right-hander Didier Fuentes then gave up Realmuto's two-run triple to the right-field corner.

Alec Bohm hit a high fastball from Sale for a run-scoring double over Harris in center in the first inning. Sale didn't give up another hit until Edmundo Sosa doubled with two outs in the fifth.

Luzardo gave up three hits with six strikeouts. He pitched longer than many expected after throwing a scoreless eighth inning in Sunday's 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays that clinched the wild-card berth.

Raisel Iglesias pitched the ninth for the save after Dylan Lee (1-0) threw a scoreless eighth.

The 37-year-old Sale threw a 100 mph fastball to Bryce Harper in the first inning. He joined Aroldis Chapman for Boston last season as the only pitchers 37 or older to throw a 100 mph pitch in the postseason since tracking began in 2008.

Braves RHP Tyler Mahle (7-10, 3.99 ERA) is expected to face Phillies LHP Cristopher Sanchez (18-7, 2.91) in Wednesday's second game of the series. Mahle was 4-1 with a 1.99 ERA in nine games with Atlanta.

stories.headline: Ex-NBA champ JR Smith arrested on assault charge in Texas
stories.summary: Former NBA champion JR Smith was arrested Monday in Texas on a charge of assault causing "bodily injury family violence."
stories.body:
Former NBA champion JR Smith was arrested Monday in Texas on a charge of assault causing "bodily injury family violence," according to jail records.

Smith, 41, was booked into Hunt County Detention Center on Monday after being arrested by the Royse City Police Department. According to jail records, Smith had a $5,000 surety bond set by a Hunt County magistrate judge Tuesday afternoon. Smith apparently remained in jail as of midday Tuesday, according to jail records.

Smith's representatives did not immediately respond to an ESPN message requesting comment.

The Royse City Police Department received an alert indicating the Southlake Police Department had issued a warrant for Smith, according to a release from Kirk Aldridge, the Royse City chief of police. Smith's license plate was spotted on Interstate 30, northeast of Dallas. Officers identified Smith and arrested him.

Smith was driving with his brother, Aldridge stated. Police released the car to Smith's brother when they arrested Smith.

In a news release Tuesday, Southlake police called Smith's arrest part of an "ongoing investigation." The police department declined to provide further information.

According to a Southlake police spokesperson, Smith will be arraigned in Tarrant County.

Southlake is northwest of Dallas.

In 2009, Smith was sentenced to 90 days in jail -- with 60 days suspended -- and 500 hours of community service for reckless driving after causing a car accident that killed one of his friends in 2007. Smith expressed remorse, telling the court in 2009 that "it's been unbearable to deal with. I'm deeply sorry," The Associated Press reported at the time.

Smith played 16 seasons in the NBA for New Orleans Hornets, Denver Nuggets, New York Knicks, Cleveland Cavaliers and Los Angeles Lakers. He last played a game in 2020 with the Lakers and averaged 12.4 points, 3.1 rebounds and 2.1 assists during his career.

He won two NBA championships as a player and was named the NBA Sixth Man of the Year in 2013. After his NBA career, Smith played college golf for North Carolina A&T. He graduated from the school in May.

stories.headline: Hard to see how Man City recover from extraordinary guilty verdict
stories.summary: Tuesday's confirmation that Manchester City were found guilty by the Premier League on over 100 breaches of financial regulations has sent shockwaves through the sport. How do Man City survive this?
stories.body:
And now it's official: according to the Premier League's three-person independent commission, Manchester City have been found guilty of inflated revenues and lowered costs through "sham" (the league's own remark) sponsorship deals, self-dealing image rights contracts with phony companies and off-the-books payments.

This inflated reporting enabled them to disguise more than £900 million ($1.18 billion) as legitimate commercial revenue over a nine-year period when, in fact, it was nothing more than the owner, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), dipping into the family coffers. In so doing, they severely breached the Financial Sustainability rules laid out by the Premier League and UEFA -- regulations they publicly endorsed and claimed to support. Along the way, among the 100+ charges they were also found guilty of false accounting -- which is somewhat inevitable when you misstate the source and scope of your income -- failing to cooperate with investigators and failing to "act in the utmost good faith." All in all, a breathtaking set of findings.

After Friday's news that City had been found guilty had broken, but was not yet official, City chairman Khaldoon Al-Mubarak issued a statement Saturday saying "our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began." He also made reference to "irrefutable evidence," which felt odd when he knew it had been refuted just 48 hours earlier by the independent commission. City are entitled to appeal the decision by this Friday, though it's worth noting that no new evidence can be brought in as part of the appeal process.

- Dawson: Man City's guilt the talk of the town in English soccer

- Premier League findings: Scope and scale of Man City's wrongdoing

- Sources: Man City learned of guilty verdicts before busy summer transfers

We are not privy to the entire judgement -- partly because it's freakishly long and dense, partly due to the Premier League's confidentiality rules -- but the 40-page "Core Decision," even with its myriad redactions, illustrates quite clearly the case against City and doesn't pull punches in terms of its language, describing City's actions as a "sham" on several occasions.

For those who have followed the case over the past 15 years, covered the settlement agreement with UEFA in 2014 when City were first punished for breaching Financial Fair Play rules (an agreement brokered by one Gianni Infantino in an earlier life) and covered the subsequent UEFA ban in February 2020 and City's successful appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) that same summer, not much of this is new. Most of it was there in Der Spiegel's investigation into the Football Leaks documents in 2018, and it was those revelations that prompted the Premier League's investigation.

What was new -- because over the past 15 years, the club has never addressed any specific charge other than to repeat ad nauseam that they were compliant with all regulations -- was some of their arguments. Most striking, perhaps, is how they justified the fact that between 2009-10 and 2017-18, they claimed to have received some £949.94 million ($1.254 billion) in commercial revenue from Abu Dhabi sponsors, but only £119.25m was actually paid by the partners themselves. The rest came from ADUG.

City's defence (76b on page 21) was that "from time to time," their commercial sponsors would apply for financial assistance from the Abu Dhabi government to meet their financial commitments, and that each time the Abu Dhabi government wired them money. Exactly, as it happened, in the amount they needed to meet their sponsor commitments to City.

ADUG, City's majority owner, is distinct and separate from the Abu Dhabi government, according to ADUG themselves. But it's not lost on anyone that ADUG's owner, Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, also happens to be a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, vice-president of the UAE and the little brother of the current president of the country.

As legal defences go, if it sounds a little desperate to you, you're not alone. The Independent Commission found that it was an "explanation" that had been "concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguise Funding Scheme."

The "Core Decision" also touches upon other City revenue obfuscation schemes. Like giving their manager at the time, Roberto Mancini, an additional contract as a consultant to one of their clubs in Abu Dhabi, thereby lowering the salary paid by City without affecting his total compensation package. Or the Fordham scheme, where ADUG sets up (and funds) a company (described in the "Core Decision" as "a front for ADUG") to buy and exploit the image rights of players from City themselves for inflated amounts.

It's worth remembering here that without the documents that were leaked by a young Portuguese guy named Rui Pinto -- who may or may not be a hacker though he has always denied it, saying he was handed the documents -- most likely none of this would have ever come to light.

So what comes next?

City will presumably lodge their appeal and, in the meantime, the Commission will issue their sanctions, which could include everything from relegation to stripped titles, from transfer freezes to massive fines and all of the above. Once the sanctions are in, a new three-person Independent Panel will convene and hear the appeal. The sanctions themselves obviously won't be enforced until the appeals process is concluded, which, judging by the glacial pace of events -- the "Core Decision" references that hearings took place in the final quarter of 2024 -- might not be until well into 2027 or beyond.

It won't end there. A number of Premier League clubs have filed legal documents to reserve the right to pursue City for compensation in the courts if they're found guilty. It's not just about lost titles -- it's about lost revenue, and City's spending driving up costs for everyone.

There is one line in the "Core Decision" that offers a little bit of hope. Maybe it's a bread crumb from the panel, suggesting what they hope the best possible outcome might be. Article 70 states that "There was no evidence that [REDACTED] authorised the operation... and so went on without his knowledge."

Who are they talking about?

Is it Khaldoon Al-Mubarak, the chairman? Could it be Mansour himself? Could it be somebody high enough up the Abu Dhabi food chain that could legitimately say: "Enough! We're obviously not getting away with this, there's no evidence that I was involved so I'm putting a stop to this. I'm calling up the Premier League and the affected clubs and their owners, most of whom are fellow billionaires anyway, I'm dumping all the responsibility on my lawyers, accountants and club executives and I'm going to see if there's a plea bargain to be had."

It's a far-fetched thought, and it's also hard to see what a plea bargain might look like -- at least one that would satisfy other clubs and their fan bases. It would need to be painful for City not just financially, but in sporting terms too. Then again, if there's one thing the owners aren't lacking it's money and, lest we forget, City's fan base -- who have endured relegation to the third flight before and come back stronger -- are resilient. But it might just offer a way out and spare the Premier League another protracted legal battle.

If not, if City lose the appeal and the acrimony continues, the knowledge that nearly a decade of Premier League football was, in many ways, a sham, is going to be a body blow. Not so much for fans of other clubs -- yes, they'll moan about lost titles and relegations and whatnot -- because most concluded a long time ago that City were guilty.

But for City fans themselves, who were lied to all this time and who put their trust in a lie. Some won't care. Many will, but we'll all have to live with the fallout.

stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
Bad blood between UFC women's bantamweight title contenders Norma Dumont and Ailin Perez boiled over during their faceoff a day ahead of Saturday's fight, with matchmaker Sean Shelby forced to keep the fighters separated from each other.

The next night, when the fight concluded with Perez announced as the winner, Dumont appeared shocked by the unanimous decision and Perez turned her back on Dumont and twerked in her direction. The fighters had to be separated again before being escorted from the cage.

The fight that happened in between those fiery moments? It was not nearly as fierce. It began with a Round 1 in which Dumont landed eight significant strikes and Perez only four. And while the action picked up a little in the two rounds that followed, the women mostly circled each other.

But Perez got the win, and as a result, she moved up two spots to No. 2 in the ESPN women's bantamweight rankings, bumping Dumont down to No. 3.

That is the only movement in the latest rankings.

stories.headline: How Lynx star Olivia Miles became the WNBA's Rookie of the Year
stories.summary: From the playgrounds in New Jersey to the WNBA's biggest stage, Olivia Miles leaves it all on the line.
stories.body:
"You can't f---ing guard me!"

That's what Olivia Miles screamed into the void at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles after beating her defender for her patented left-handed finger roll and drawing a foul.

"The Spectacle," a nickname that has gained momentum in recent weeks, pounded her chest and high-fived teammates. Then, she calmly walked to the free throw line -- as if someone else had shown that emotion.

"In a way, it's like a different persona that I embody," Miles told ESPN. "But I've learned a lot from Kobe [Bryant] and his mentality. He had to develop that to be as successful as he was and to tap into that killer mode. I think it's so important if you want to achieve things at the highest level, you have to have that mental toughness and that supreme confidence that no one can touch you at any given moment."

Miles, who was named the unanimous WNBA Rookie of the Year on Monday, has been a fiery, 5-foot-10 star for the Minnesota Lynx, who will fight to prolong their season Tuesday against the No. 8 seed New York Liberty.

As the Lynx, the No. 1 seed and odds-on favorites to win the WNBA championship going into the playoffs, attempt to stave off elimination, Miles is the centerpiece of that ambition. Lynx fans haven't been this giddy about a young talent since Maya Moore, who broke their hearts by retiring in 2018 when she was just 29 years old.

Fan support for Miles multiplied when she carried the Lynx as former MVP candidate Napheesa Collier recovered from a pair of offseason ankle surgeries. With Collier out and a revamped Lynx roster learning to jell, Miles -- the second pick in the 2026 WNBA draft -- soared, breaking records once held by Caitlin Clark and other first-year stars who hit the ground running.

Miles became the first WNBA player to record at least 45 points and 20 assists in their first three games. By mid-June, she tied Paige Bueckers' WNBA record as the fastest player in league history to reach 250-plus points and 50-plus assists. Before the team's two-game losing streak that preceded the FIBA World Cup break in August, Miles had helped the Lynx win 16 of 17 games. She also reached at least 400 points, 100 rebounds and 100 assists in 26 games, faster than any other player in league history. No WNBA rookie has come this close to on-court supremacy since Candace Parker won WNBA MVP honors and Rookie of the Year in 2008 while leading her team to the Western Conference finals.

"She's different, right? The way she sees the game, her basketball IQ," said WNBA All-Star Courtney Williams, who is enjoying the most efficient offensive season of her 11-year career. "I mean, you never see a rookie coming in doing the things that she's doing, so that speaks for itself."

Miles is, by all accounts, laid back off the court. She loves naps, her cat and playing video games on a quiet Friday night.

On the court, she balances her ability to pull off viral touch passes, up-and-under layups and half-court 3-pointers -- all learned on playgrounds and pickup courts in New Jersey -- with her competitiveness and East Coast energy, and when to show that side of her personality.

"It's an attitude more than anything," said Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve, who added that she tries to pretend she's not in awe of some of Miles' moves. "The players, I've heard them comment, 'You can't take the Jersey out of her.' I feel the same. I'm at home with [Miles] in her ways and some of the edge that she competes with, and she doesn't take anything from anybody. I think it's that mindset, physical toughness, certainly, the mental toughness. I think it's more of that than a basketball style play."

JUST DON'T GET hit in the face.

That was the message Abby Brown heard from her parents when the fourth grader from down the street in Phillipsburg, New Jersey, joined the Lady Liners AAU fifth grade team.

Miles, the youngest player on the team, became known almost immediately as the elementary school savant who zipped passes that were more advanced for her age.

"One game, I thought she was going for the layup because her eyes were focused on the rim," Brown recalled. "And then, I got slammed in the chest with the ball. Everyone just kind of knew. You just didn't know when she was going to make a pass. You just had to be ready."

Miles' unselfish approach made everyone love her, Brown said. Brown and Miles carpooled to tournaments, had fun on sleepovers and enjoyed weekend trips to the beach. But Brown said she also knew the moment on the court when that reserved young girl would become someone else -- someone no opponent wanted to meet.

"If you saw her off the court, you wouldn't think that she's going to go out there and absolutely kick your butt because she was just really chill," said Brown, who played with Miles through middle school. "But yeah, the second she'd gone there, you could see the intensity in her eyes once that game started. Then, you're in for it."

By sixth grade, Miles had moved up to the eighth grade team. Susan Dvorin, who coached the team, was hesitant to start Miles, fearing backlash from the parents of the older players. It took only a few games, however, for them to see that Miles was the best player on the roster. She was also like an assistant coach, telling Dvorin about gaps in the opposing team's defense and opportunities to exploit them.

"I swear she could have coached the game herself as a sixth grader," she said.

Her selflessness -- the same trait that helped Miles rank seventh in the WNBA in assists (6.0 per game) and turned her into an offensive catalyst responsible for the Lynx's 117 points per 100 possessions when she's on the floor, per databallr.com -- impressed the coach more than the rest of her game.

"After one particular game, I said, 'Olivia, you really need to shoot more,'" Dvorin said. "She had such potential for high scoring. She said, 'Coach, I don't want to be seen as a ball hog. I really like passing the ball.'"

Her talent intimidated Helena Friend, Miles' high school teammate who also played four years at Pepperdine. They were roommates at Blair Academy in Blairstown Township, New Jersey, which is where Friend learned that Miles was more soft-spoken and introverted than Friend had realized. But she and her teammates knew that once they were on court, anyone could go viral for the wrong reasons.

"We would always make jokes like, 'Oh, whose ankle is she going to break today?'" Friend said. "Over time, everyone would come into the gym and watch our practices, and we were all trying not to be on the highlight reel."

MILES' ATHLETIC GIFTS also helped David Mamukelashvili, Miles' soccer coach at Blair Academy.

Miles, who left the school just two goals shy of the Blair Academy career record after COVID-19 canceled her senior season, was pretty good at soccer, too. She was also committed.

During the recruiting process, a top college basketball coach appeared at Miles' soccer practice, ready to take her to dinner. Miles said the coach had to wait until she was done with soccer, even though Mamukelashvili told her she could leave early.

"She's like, 'Sorry, I need to finish my practice,'" Mamukelashvili said.

On Sundays, the team's off day, Miles would often call her soccer coach and ask him to practice penalty kicks with her. Some people told Miles to stay away from soccer and focus on basketball for fear of injury. She refused, believing the training helped her in both sports.

"I think a lot of it is the agility and the way you move and glide in soccer; it's different," Miles said. "It's very angelic in a way. It's like you have to move gracefully all over the pitch and then obviously on the court. But I think it really helped my passing because in soccer, you have to find windows, you have to lead people places, you have to anticipate a lot of things."

Such as the elbows opponents would throw at her during matches. They also pulled her jersey to irk her. That made Mamukelashvili anxious because he knew he'd have to manage his star.

"She was a player who was so good that she had to endure a lot of physical battles, and I had to calm her down sometimes because she's like, 'This girl is all over me, and they're not calling it,'" Mamukelashvili said.

Miles would respond to the cheap shots with trash talk. She'd score a goal and stare down an opponent or put a finger on her mouth to silence an opposing crowd. Mamukelashvili, midgame, would sometimes hear from administrators who wanted Miles to tone things down. He'd nod but still allow Miles to play her way.

"There are some coaches in high school who are like, 'This is just high school level. Let's keep it chill and low-key and be respectful of the other teams,'" he said. "But, honestly, I loved it."

Years later, the Minnesota Lynx do, too.

DeWANNA BONNER WASN'T sure what she had just witnessed after Miles skated through four Phoenix Mercury defenders for a left-handed layup during a road loss to the Lynx in July.

Over her 17 seasons, Bonner has played against Diana Taurasi, Maya Moore and Candace Parker. But when Miles carved up the Mercury earlier this season -- she and teammate Kayla McBride combined for 70 points in that game -- the veteran wasn't sure she had ever seen what that was. "She reads the game very, very well for a rookie, and she knows when to attack; she knows when to shoot," Bonner said. "She knows when to get her teammates involved, and that's just unheard of, the IQ she has as a rookie."

"I think the season before last season, I think what made [the Lynx] so difficult to guard was their ability to move the ball," said WNBA all-star Alyssa Thomas, who averaged 20.3 points when the Mercury eliminated the Lynx in the 2025 playoffs. "And I think they're back to doing that. You can't just focus on one person. Now, the ball is snapping around, and you have to play for everybody. You don't know who's going to take the shots, and I think that's what makes them dangerous."

In that win over the Mercury in Minneapolis, Miles darted through Phoenix defenders, wowing an adoring fanbase with every behind-the-back pass, fast-break bucket and step-back 3-pointer. She sealed the win by flicking a pass to McBride in the corner that curved around the arc and landed in the veteran's hands for a 3-pointer.

"I'm much more comfortable in those spaces and where [Miles] is finding me, and with the speed and the velocity the ball comes at now, I'm able to capitalize on it," said McBride, who is shooting a career-high 42% from the 3-point line this season. "It's just been a lot of fun. It's a kid in the candy store. As a hooper, you can't ask for much more than having a point guard that's just looking for you."

And McBride is only one of the beneficiaries of the breathtaking East Coast point guard who has added even more pizzazz to the thriving league with a flair, intensity and skill set few rookies in WNBA history have matched.

"[Miles] doing this and shouldering so much, basically the entire team -- the success of the team is on her shoulders," Reeve said. "That is impressive how she's handled it."

And now, at the biggest moment of their season, the Lynx will rely on her again. The rookie with the goggles who might dribble past an opponent and scream when they fall, who can turn it all off and on like a faucet in those crucial moments, is playing the second game of her postseason career with everything on the line. And no one worries whether she'll find a competitive edge.

"If I see something or if I feel the game going a certain way, then I can feel it coming on," Miles said. "I use all of my energy here, my adrenaline; I channel it in the right ways. I'm not perfect, but I'm learning how to use the energy for good and to rile up my teammates and to get everyone going -- and to get myself going, too."

stories.headline: Ferrari gives Fred Vasseur 'full confidence' amid Christian Horner speculation
stories.summary: Ferrari has insisted it has "full confidence" in Fred Vasseur amid mounting speculation about both his job and the potential of Christian Horner replacing him.
stories.body:
Ferrari has insisted it has "full confidence" in Fred Vasseur amid mounting speculation about both his job and the potential of Christian Horner replacing him.

In a hastily-arranged virtual news conference on Tuesday, Ferrari's chief communication officer Maria Conti said the team -- under-pressure due to poor results on the track -- wanted to avoid any "gossip" moving forwards.

"We have confidence -- full confidence -- in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so," she said. "At this time it's really important that the team remains united and cohesive, and we are focused with all the energy on the work ahead.

"Ferrari has always attracted extraordinary interest, and it's only natural that many professionals aspire to be part of it. It is a reflection of the strength of what Ferrari really represents.

"So, this is why we really want to avoid, and we do not intend to fuel speculation or comment on assumptions coming from outside the company.

"And it's not just related to the story in the times of Mr. Horner, but in general, the speculation about Fred."

An interview Horner had given The Times, published ahead of last weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, took on a life of its own ahead of the Baku event. Horner's interview, which had been primarily to promote his new autobiography, out next month, included a response to a question about whether he would take the Ferrari job.

Horner replied: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."

Sources have told ESPN the former Red Bull boss was not intending to use the Times interview to declare his interest in Vasseur's job, and that he is not actively pursuing a job with the Italian job as things stand, nor has he been offered one. Either way, the quote dominated the build-up and aftermath of the Baku race.

After Saturday's event, a frustrated Vasseur said he had been asked "25 times a day" about his job and the Horner link.

The speculation around Vasseur and Ferrari leadership has reached fever pitch recently as the team's performances have slumped.

Earlier this month, Lewis Hamilton posted to Instagram to deny multiple reports in Italy that he was pushing for changes to be made to senior members of the race team -- the seven-time world champion said he still backed Vasseur after the Baku race.

Tuesday's press conference comes ahead of a race in Malaysia -- F1 is in the middle of the first of three triple headers (nine races across 11 weekends) to close out the season Conti added that while news about Ferrari is not uncommon, it was time to draw a line in the sand underneath it so the team can focus on the remainder of the season.

- Lando Norris apologises to Franco Colapinto after calling for ban

- Russell's win won't kick-start title challenge, but Baku rewards his faith in trying 2026

- Charles Leclerc admits Ferrari's rivals have taken 'big steps forwards': 'We must not lie to ourselves'

"We are doing that today, on Tuesday 29th of September, because we would like to avoid that the next weekend in Malaysia will be focused only on this kind of gossip and speculation. But we would like to be focused on the race, on the performance, on the team, on Fred," Conti added.

"The storm of communication around the team -- we are used to that, Ferrari is used to that.

"With more than 21 social media channels covering all the company, the fact is that after the race and on Sunday and yesterday, we can say this storm of communication was increasing. Normally it's going down.

"And as we have a race the next weekend in Malaysia, we would like to take the time to ask you kindly not to focus on this. Fred is in his position and we are confirming his leadership. And we would like to be focused on the race, the team and its leadership.

"This is why we have done it. Because looking and monitoring the communication yesterday, today, normally it's going down. But everybody, not just you guys, but also Italian media from all over the world, they are still creating a lot of different stories around Fred.

"And this is not useful. So this is why we decided to do that."

Vassuer has been Ferrari boss since 2023 and almost led the team to a constructors' championship the following season, narrowly missing out to McLaren. He played an instrumental role in signing Hamilton to the team at the start of 2025.

Ferrari started this season looking like the closest challengers to the dominant Mercedes team. Lewis Hamilton won in Spain before Charles Leclerc won in Great Britain, but the team's results have dried up recently. Ferrari has not been on the podium at any of the last five races.

stories.headline: Tasmania Devils unveil top teenagers as first signings
stories.summary: Eight teenagers, including a highly fancied Western Australian youngster, have become the Tasmania Devils' maiden AFL signings.
stories.body:
Highly touted Western Australian youngster Axel Walsh, a host of Victorians and one local talent have been snapped up by the Tasmania Devils as their first signings.

The club, which will enter the AFL and AFLW in 2028, on Tuesday night revealed eight under-17 players it had signed as part of its list-concession build.

Tasmania can sign up to 12 pre-draft 17-year-old players across 2026 and 2027, taking them out of the AFL draft.

Top of the tree was Walsh, an athletic 202cm forward-ruck who averaged 12.8 disposals and 10.3 hitouts and kicked three goals in four matches at the most recent under-18 carnival.

He was likely to be the No.1 pick in the 2027 draft.

Victorians Jake Miller, Angus Brown, Riley Stratford, Baxter Sruk, Griffin Barker and Nate Jenkins have also joined.

Miller, at 197cm, has been described as a regular goal kicker at club and school level, Brown has a zippy running game, while midfielder Sruk has an ability to rack up possessions.

Tasmanian draft prospect Hugh McCallum, who was sidelined this season with a knee injury, has also been signed.

A lightly-framed wingman or half-forward, McCallum is the brother of former Port Adelaide-listed defender Tom McCallum.

The Devils will be hoping the group can follow the lead of Jeremy Cameron, Dylan Shiel and Adam Treloar, who forged successful careers after being signed by the Giants through the same concession rules prior to their inaugural 2012 season.

"It's a proud moment to welcome our first group of Tasmania Devils players to our state," coach Ken Hinkley said in a club statement.

"I am excited to be working with such a talented group of young footballers, all of whom have tremendous skill sets and AFL attributes already."

McCallum was the final player announced - etching his name in history as the first native Devils contracted player.

"I'm stoked to be a part of it. Growing up you used to have to go to the mainland to play AFL," he said.

Players were assessed at national championships, school and local matches, and were benchmarked against their age group.

All pre-listed players will move to the state in November and begin their preparation for 2028 with individualised training programs.

The under-17 concessions are among the generous list-build options available to the Devils, who also have seven first-round draft picks in 2027 including the first and the third.

stories.headline: Five stats: Why USMNT should be excited about Cavan Sullivan
stories.summary: Is the hype around Cavan Sullivan's USMNT future too much? No, it's actually not enough -- and here are five reasons why.
stories.body:
There's something incredible happening in MLS right now, and the average World Cup watcher probably has no clue.

Seriously, think about all of the people you know who are "sports fans" but maybe not "soccer fans" -- the ones who root hard for the U.S. men's national team every four years and know the names of their four or five best players.

Sure, they probably still can't pronounce the last name of manager Mauricio Pochettino, but they watched tons of soccer this summer. The World Cup had so many games, and finally, it was all aligned with our time zones. These people now have opinions about VAR, England's prevent defense and the general moral fiber of the Argentina national team.

They're primed to care about soccer, especially American soccer, and especially a kind of greatness we've never seen before from a player of a certain age. No, I'm not talking about Lionel Messi, who somehow (1) might still be the greatest soccer player in the world, (2) is easily the greatest 39-year-old soccer player we've ever seen, and (3) continues to play soccer every week, across North America, without having any effect on North American sports discourse.

No, I'm talking about Cavan Sullivan, the 16-year-old phenom who, somehow, still feels as if he's being underhyped.

The history of American soccer is filled with players who were overpromised and couldn't do anything but underdeliver, but this is different. It's not just that we, Americans, have never seen someone like Sullivan. No, the wider soccer world -- the rest of the entire world -- rarely ever sees someone like Sullivan.

Here are some numbers for why you should get excited:

1,675 minutes
As I like to often say: The best predictor of future stardom is minutes players at a young age.

Take the three front-runners for this year's Ballon d'Or. Harry Kane was playing and scoring goals for Millwall in the Championship during his age-18 season. Lamine Yamal is 19 -- right now. And Kylian Mbappé broke out for Monaco during his age-17 season.

Sullivan is currently in his age-16 season (defined by your age at the start of the campaign). And so far, he has played 1,675 league minutes in MLS.

The site FBref has data for what they call the "Next 14" -- essentially, the most competitive leagues in the world after Europe's Big Five -- that goes back to the beginning of the current century, if not more. Only 21 outfield players have played more league minutes than Sullivan, who still has at least eight games left in his season. If we expand the dataset to include the Big Five, then only five other players -- Eduardo Camavinga, Alex Song, Gavi, Lamine Yamal, and Nuri Sahin -- have played more minutes than Sullivan before their age-17 season.

The leader, among all of these players? Freddy Adu had played 5,448 minutes by the end of his age-16 season.

€1.54 billion
Though we don't have much useful leaguewide data dating to 2006, when Adu was wrapping up his age-16 season, I do feel confident in saying the following: MLS is a lot better than it was 20 years ago.

Heck, it's a lot better than it was even 10 years ago. Per a recent analysis by Michael Caley: In 2016, the average combined transfer value of the median MLS team (as estimated by the site Transfermarkt) was significantly lower than the average team in the first divisions in Mexico, Belgium, Portugal and the Netherlands. Since then, the league has essentially caught up to Belgium and Mexico in transfer value, and it has surpassed Portugal and the Netherlands.

Though the biggest teams in those European leagues are still way better and richer than any MLS side -- thanks to Champions League prize money -- the average match that Cavan Sullivan plays in MLS is probably tougher than what he'd face were he playing for Benfica, Porto or PSV.

All in all, the combined estimated transfer values of all 30 MLS clubs is €1.54 billion -- or about €51.3 million per team.

12 goals and assists
For the Big Five leagues, FBref has goal-and-assist data dating to at least the mid-1990s for Ligue 1, for the entirety of the Premier League since its breakaway from the English Football League in 1992, and the late 1980s for Italy, Germany and Spain.

Over that stretch, the record for goals+assists before a player's age-17 season comes from Bojan Krkic, who scored 10 goals and created three more in his early years -- right at the beginning of Pep Guardiola's dominance with Barcelona. Next after him is a tie between Yamal and Wayne Rooney's Everton years, at 10.

Sullivan currently has 12 -- a nearly even split between seven goals and five assists. If we expand the list out to the Next 14 leagues, then only four players have more. Chelsea's Estêvão registered 23 goal contributions with Palmeiras in Brazil's top flight -- a much tougher league than MLS. Normally, I'd remove penalties from the equation, but the fact that Estevao was chosen to take three penalties as a 16-year-old feels like useful information.

Then there's Adu with 22, Romelu Lukaku with 19 for Anderlecht, and Endrick's 15 with Palmeiras before he moved to Real Madrid.

The smart money is on Sullivan moving up the list over the next month as MLS wraps up its regular season. In his eight games since the World Cup, he has scored six goals and added four assists.

132 passes into the attacking third
Sullivan is the rare attacking prospect whose attacking production actually underrates his track record.

Of course, the production at this point in his career is fantastic -- bested only by a collection of some of the best attacking prospects of the past 30 years. But that production is backed up by a sustainable drumbeat of quality shots and chances created, plus a bedrock of excellent ball progression and off-ball movement.

To dig into some more advanced numbers, we need to move beyond FBref's historical database. Stats Perform doesn't have numbers that extend to the 1990s, but we're able to look at the Big Five in Europe, MLS, Liga MX, the Dutch Eredivisie, the English second division, a number of cup competitions in Europe and South America, plus the first divisions in Portugal, Brazil, Argentina and Colombia. The data dates to at least the mid-2010s.

Among all of the players who fall within there, Sullivan ranks third and second, respectively, in the two most important and predictive attacking metrics: expected goals and expected assists. The other players I've highlighted in the below chart, which only looks at minutes played at age 16 or earlier, mostly played in more difficult leagues, but across the modern era of the sport almost no one has done what Sullivan is currently doing, still eight years away from the start of his prime:

He's also not just standing up near the goal and waiting for things to happen. Among this same cohort, Sullivan leads all players in passes played into the attacking third, with 132. The only other players with more than 100 are Jude Bellingham (104) and Gilberto Mora (109), both of whom are midfielders, not attackers.

That's clear when we look at passes played into the penalty area. Both Mora and Bellingham landed right around 100; Sullivan is all the way up at 202. Only Yamal, at 254, played more.

Scoring goals, creating chances, moving the ball into the attacking third, moving the ball into the box -- that's all there. The only thing missing is an ability to find space off of the ball, and it's only missing because I haven't mentioned it yet.

Sullivan has taken 142 touches inside the box. Among this cohort, Yamal, again, is the only player with more.

78 rating
The best players in modern soccer are the wide attackers who score goals, create chances, move the ball into attacking positions and find space inside the box. The best attacking prospects -- players in their late teens and early 20s -- tend to be able to score and create goals at a young age, but that's it. They usually can't aid in buildup play -- outside of slowing things down with a succession of head-down dribbles that sometimes move the ball upfield but often kill attacks by allowing the defense to recover. And they rarely have an advanced enough understanding of space and ball movement to be patient and savvy enough to receive passes in dangerous positions.

This all-conquering winger is a new prototype of player -- so new that the two best examples, Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, are still playing. And so we haven't seen many young players develop with this idea in mind. That is, until Yamal -- and yes, now Sullivan.

The just-turned-17-year-old doesn't just have good-for-a-16-year-old numbers in his first real professional season. No, he genuinely has been one of the best players in MLS.

The player-rating model from the stats app Futi looks at how much every touch increases or decreases his team's chances of scoring and conceding a goal. Then it adjusts for the player's role and how well his team plays when he's on and off the field. And finally, they convert it all into an easy-to-understand 0-to-100 scale.

Among players with at least 1,500 minutes played this season, Sullivan currently ranks in the top 10 for the Futi model. The average age of the players ahead of him is nearly twice his: 31. And that's all for the full season; if we looked only at the post-World-Cup stretch, he probably would be even higher:

There are still plenty of questions.

Will he grow? What happens when he has moved beyond Philadelphia's relatively chaotic system? How might he handle moving and living in Europe? Those questions -- and more -- would hold true for any 16-year-old soccer player.

But while it probably won't happen because it's an unlikely outcome for everyone who has ever lived, Sullivan's early-career excellence means that he is more likely to become a superstar than any American who has come before him.

Just consider this. Futi also rates each individual area of a player's in-possession performance: shooting, creating, receiving, dribbling and linking (or buildup play). There are two players in the league who rate above a 60 in all five.

The two: Cavan Sullivan and Lionel Messi.

stories.headline: Crossland banned four games for Cleary tackle
stories.summary: Newcastle's Phoenix Crossland will miss the NRL grand final and most of the World Cup after receiving a four-match ban for his hip-drop tackle on Nathan Cleary.
stories.body:
Newcastle forward Phoenix Crossland apologised to "everyone" in rugby league as the NRL judiciary handed him a four-match ban for the hip-drop tackle that broke the leg of his favourite player, Penrith's Nathan Cleary.

During 85 minutes of evidence on Tuesday night at the NRL's Moore Park headquarters, Crossland said the incident had taken the focus off grand final week.

"Apologies to everyone involved in the game. I hope after tonight we can get back to the football," he said, holding back tears.

"If I could change the circumstances in any way, I would."

The suspension over the tackle in Newcastle's win over the Panthers in last Sunday's preliminary final, means Crossland will not only miss this Sunday's grand final against the Sydney Roosters but also the majority of the World Cup for New Zealand.

Crossland, who has played six Tests for New Zealand, will now miss all three pool games for the Kiwis against Australia, the Cook Islands and Fiji. New Zealand would have to make the semi-finals for him to feature.

The 26 year-old emerged from the hearing to make a statement without taking questions.

"I want to thank everybody inside for a fair hearing. I apologise to Nathan and the Panthers and more importantly to the game and the fans," he said.

"It's a terrible start to the most important week of the year due to myself.

"As soon as I walk out this building my focus goes to the Newcastle Knights and winning this grand final, helping Harrison Graham prepare as best he can and get a win on Sunday."

Graham stepped into the hooking role against the Panthers after Crossland was sent off and has been named on the bench for Sunday.

Crossland also revealed he had contacted Cleary and his father, Penrith coach Ivan Cleary, to apologise.

"It was a tough phone call and I just wanted to reach out and apologise," Crossland told Judiciary chair Geoffrey Bellew and panel members Ryan James and Paul Simpkins.

"It's been the worst couple of days of my life.

"He's my favourite player by a mile and the only reason he's in hospital is because of me.

"He was such a gentleman and told me not to worry and to stop saying sorry because these things just happen.

"He is a class act."

Knights counsel James McLeod had asked for a penalty of no more than three matches but said a two-game ban would be appropriate given Crossland had shown deep remorse and pleaded guilty.

NRL counsel Patrick Knowles SC said that while there were mitigating circumstances, a penalty of four matches was appropriate, comparing it to a four-game ban handed to St George Illawarra prop Ryan Couchman earlier this year.

His hip-drop tackle on Parramatta's J'maine Hopgood resulted in a season-ending ACL tear.

Cleary's injury was one of the worst suffered on an NRL field this season.

He underwent emergency surgery in Sydney's Royal North Shore Hospital on Sunday night.

Cleary is also Australia's incumbent halfback but will also miss the four-week World Cup, which starts on October 15.

The Knights submitted two character references for Crossland from 2001 premiership coach Michael Hagan and club legend Mark Hughes.

McLeod also drew attention to the fact Crossland had played 132 games for the Knights but never a grand final.

But Bellew said the game's judiciary code did not distinguish between matches.

"The fact a grand final will be missed is irrelevant," he said.

Crossland's 1077 tackles this year are the most of any player in the NRL, with the incident on Cleary only the second time he had been charged in 2026.

Tuesday night's decision came after Cleary called out those peppering the embattled Knight with social-media abuse and threats.

"Please don't be one of those people writing comments like this to Phoenix," Cleary posted alongside a graphic of some of the abuse Crossland had received.

"It was a complete accident and he doesn't deserve the unwarranted hate. He reached out to apologise and I have nothing but respect for him.

"He's a competitor and our game is made up of split-second moments that sometimes lead to unfortunate circumstances.

"Comments like this are so unfair. Spread love, not hate."

stories.headline: Patriots place offensive lineman Greg Van Roten (thigh) on IR
stories.summary: The Patriots placed guard Greg Van Roten on injured reserve Tuesday as the infrastructure around quarterback Drake Maye took another hit.
stories.body:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Infrastructure around struggling quarterback Drake Maye took another hit Tuesday when the New England Patriots placed veteran guard Greg Van Roten on injured reserve -- another reminder that the team's run of good health contributing to its surprising run to Super Bowl LX hasn't carried into 2026.

Van Roten, who started in Sunday's blowout loss to the Jaguars in place of opening-day starter Mike Onwenu (broken ankle), is the 17th player the Patriots have placed on injured reserve and/or reached an injury settlement with this season. Last season, the Patriots placed 16 players on injured reserve all season.

Among the 17 players the Patriots have placed on injured reserve include Onwenu, No. 1 receiver A.J. Brown, No. 2 tight end Julian Hill, top backup safety Dell Pettus, top backup offensive tackle Marcus Bryant and punter Bryce Baringer.

Van Roten, 36, was knocked out of Sunday's game in the second quarter with a thigh injury, according to the team.

Maye, who threw two interceptions and lost a fumble in the game, faced a 47% pressure rate, according to ESPN Research. That is the highest rate he's faced this season and the fourth highest of his three-year career.

Maye went 4-of-9 with an interception when pressured Sunday and has completed 41% of his passes under pressure this season, with no touchdowns and three interceptions, according to ESPN Research.

Head coach Mike Vrabel foreshadowed Monday that the Patriots were preparing to be without Van Roten when he said backup center Ben Brown would likely take repetitions at right guard this week. When Van Roten left Sunday's game, third-year veteran Walter Rouse -- who was acquired from the Minnesota Vikings on Aug. 30 -- took his place.

The Patriots had signed Van Roten, who is in his 12th NFL season, to a one-year, $3 million contract on Aug.18.

The Patriots (1-2) visit the AFC East rival Buffalo Bills (3-0) on Sunday.

stories.headline: NBA preseason buzz: Latest on trades, news and intel
stories.summary: The NBA regular season is less than a month away, and we're tracking all the news, deals, and trades across the league.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 NBA season officially kicked off Sept. 22 as the Houston Rockets held their media day, before the Dallas Mavericks followed suit Friday.

The other 28 teams in the association joined them Monday, ahead of training camps beginning for most teams.

How will LeBron James and Jaylen Brown look in their new Philadelphia 76ers uniforms? What will Giannis Antetokounmpo's first media day away from Milwaukee look like? And how will the other new faces in new places make their first impressions?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions | Offseason buzz

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Sept. 29

Charania: NBA reviewing finalists' bids for Vegas team

ESPN's Shams Charania reported that the NBA is currently reviewing finalist bids for a new expansion team in Las Vegas. The price range is currently speculated at $12-13 billion with a new arena factored into the cost.

The three final groups are Nancy Walton Laurie and Bill Laurie; Steve Apostolopoulos and Marc Lasry; Bill Foley and Jerry Colangelo, sources told ESPN.

Embiid "full participant" in first Sixers' practice
Joel Embiid was a "full participant all the way through" for the Philadelphia 76ers first practice of training camp, Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Tuesday.

"He looked great," Nurse said of Embiid. "Very, very good news from the standpoint of where it's been the last couple years, last couple summers leading into today. ... It's great to see."

After being named the league MVP in 2023, the 32-year-old center has missed 150 games over the last three seasons because of various injuries.

He also sat out four of the Sixers' 11 playoff games in the spring because of appendicitis, right hip soreness and a right ankle sprain.

The only Sixers player who did not participate in Tuesday's practice according to a team spokesperson was backup big man Adem Bona, who is dealing with a sprained left foot.

Anfernee Simons, who signed a two-year, $12.3 million contract to join Philadelphia in July, said Embiid's presence in the gym was already notable leading up to the start of camp.

"Everybody's been impressed around here about how he's come in and worked," Simons said. "Joel is going to be Joel. He's going to be a dominant player always. We just want to continue for him to be himself, as well, and I think everybody's going to be able to work around that."

Despite the injuries, the 10-year veteran still averaged 26.9 points, 7.7 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 1.2 blocks per game last season.

Embiid's inclusion only added to what several Sixers players described as an "exciting" opening day with LeBron James and Jaylen Brown completing their first official practice with the franchise.

"With any team, we got to start somewhere, and then we got to get better and better, and just keep trying to reach our ceiling, right?" Nurse said. "That happens day-to-day. Can we get up tomorrow, like, 98% as excited as we did today? It's going to be hard to get as excited as we all were today, right?

"But we need to come back, and we need to keep climbing that mountain. That's a daily process. I just want them to reach their potential. If they do, great things are going to happen." -- Dave McMenamin

Hoop Collective: The 2026 NBA Media Day reaction special

Brian Windhorst is joined by ESPN reporters from around the league to check in on Monday's Media Days. Tim MacMahon, Dave McMenamin, Vince Goodwill, Jamal Collier, Anthony Slater and Michael C. Wright all hop on the podcast to discuss the biggest storylines throughout the NBA ahead of training camp.

Goodwill on the latest between the Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns: "It wasn't so much what he said, like this full-throated defense of himself, but he said, 'I would like to get my contract done.'

"He said, 'I would like to stay in New York for the rest of my career.' And then he kind of ended it and because of the way the Knicks operated, it wasn't like you had space for a follow-up.

"And then someone else, I think Ian Begley asked him, 'Are you OK with playing this out through the season or do you want to table contract talks?' and he basically said, 'Everybody's going to be a little uncomfortable around here.'"

Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path'

Sept. 28

Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path'

When LeBron James chose to leave the Los Angeles Lakers in free agency over the summer, he consulted his family on the decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers. But when it came to his son/teammate Bronny, much was apparently left unsaid.

"We're men of very little words when it comes to talking about business and what we're going to do and how we feel about each other. So it wasn't really much [discussion] to be honest with you," Bronny James said Monday at Lakers media day.

"He's got his own path and I got my own. He knows that I want to make a name for myself and I want to continue my career and keep growing as a player. And he knows that I want to focus on that. So he decided to do that."

LeBron and Bronny have routinely been in unique situations in league history, whether it was opening night two years ago, when the father and son entered the game together, or last year in the playoffs, where they combined to deliver a 10-0 run during a victory over the Houston Rockets. Navigating a complex free agency in which the father leaves and the son stays is another one for the books.

Tatum 'comfortable' leading new-look Celtics post-Brown trade

Jayson Tatum's one constant during his development into a star with the Boston Celtics was having Jaylen Brown as a teammate.

That partnership ended this offseason when the Celtics' front office decided to trade Brown -- the 2024 NBA Finals MVP -- to the Philadelphia 76ers in what was largely a cost-cutting move that broke up the duo most responsible for leading Boston to the 2024 NBA championship.

"The business of the NBA comes and plays a part at some point. And I've seen it in my almost 10 years in this league," Tatum said during Celtics media day on Monday. "For me it's more so being grateful for what we accomplished and what he means for this city and to this organization. Just the ups and downs in our career that we were able to grow and learn from and made us the players that we are today. So really just being thankful for those nine years."

Suns owner Ishbia says mortgage company woes won't hurt team
It's well-known at this point that billionaire Mat Ishbia's mortgage company has had a rough financial stretch.

The owner of the Phoenix Suns said Monday that will have "zero" effect on his spending habits when it comes to basketball. In fact, the 46-year-old said he's working on purchasing 14% more of the team, bringing his total to roughly 80%.

Ishbia's company -- United Wholesale Mortgage -- suffered a reported $450 million net loss in the second quarter this year, calling into question if the sizable dip would affect his basketball business. The outspoken Ishbia was adamant that nothing would change for the NBA franchise when it comes to spending on players or the fan experience.

Williamson not where he wants to be
New Orleans Pelicans forward Zion Williamson kept his answer brief when asked how he would summarize his first seven years as an NBA player.
"I'm not where I want to be," said Williamson, whom the Pelicans drafted with the No. 1 pick out of Duke in 2019. "I'm not where I need to be."

Butler indicates he is 'ahead' in his knee rehab

Nearing the eight-month mark since his right ACL surgery, Jimmy Butler III is hesitant to put a specific target date on his eventual NBA return, but he did express optimism in advance of Golden State Warriors training camp.

"I promise you I'm coming back, and it's going to be -- I think it's going to be, like, real eye-popping for everybody how I'm still going to be nice," Butler said. "Probably nicer, honestly."

Butler has only recently advanced to running, and he will be limited to light on-court individual work when the team begins practice in Hawaii on Tuesday afternoon.

It will be several weeks before Butler is expected to advance to a more rigorous stage of his rehab, and the team's lead medical decision-maker, Rick Celebrini, is known for his cautiousness in the later stages of the rehab process.

A January or February return can be considered on the optimistic side for Butler, who turned 37 earlier this month. But Butler did say that the strengthening tests on the knee indicate he is ahead of schedule.

"My numbers are staggering," Butler said. "They're off the charts. I'm ahead, so they say. So, I just know that all the work that I've been doing, whether it be at home, in L.A., in Europe, in South America, wherever the case may be, I've been doing all the right things. So, I am confident that whenever I come back, I'll be more than ready, I'll be more than healthy and I'll be a better all-around player than I was whenever I went down." -- Anthony Slater

Pistons eye "better version" of Cunningham

Detroit Pistons coach J.B. Bickerstaff has held many offseason conversations with All-NBA guard Cade Cunningham about seizing greatness and the necessary steps toward improving after last year's playoff run that stretched to Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals.

Bickerstaff has guaranteed "a better version" Cunningham this season, which could be a scary sight after he averaged 23.9 points, 9.9 assists, 5.5 rebounds and 1.4 steals in 33.9 minutes during 2025-26. But Cunningham also led the East in turnovers per game after finishing with the second most in 2024-25.

"I don't have to challenge Cade, and that's why he is who he is," Bickerstaff said. "Because he's pulling. He's not being pushed."

Cunningham showed up in a fresh pair of Nike S.T. Charge "Detroit Tough" sneakers in Pistons colors. He will also receive his own signature Nike shoe, which is expected to debut during the second half of the season.

"I'm thankful to be in these shoes. I'm thankful to have the opportunity to represent my family in this way," Cunningham said. "Represent where I come from, but then to represent the city of Detroit.

"In a city like this, it's a blessing. I'm thankful for it, I don't take it for granted and I'm trying to make the most out of it." -- Eric Woodyard

Hornets waive former No. 8 pick Dillingham

The Charlotte Hornets are waiving guard Rob Dillingham, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Dillingham was traded from the Chicago Bulls on Saturday for Buddy Hield and cash. The Hornets created a $9.6 million trade exception with the move.

Dillingham, 21, appeared in 30 games for the Bulls last season, averaging 9.6 points and 2.8 assists.

SGA on chance at historic third straight MVP

At Oklahoma City Thunder media day, guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander discussed the possibility of winning a third straight NBA MVP award and whether that's something he ponders going into this season.

"No different than any other year: Try to be the best player I can be, try to implement the things I just worked on," Gilgeous-Alexander said.

"The decision for MVP is literally 82 games away. I'm not going to win the award in the first week of the season. ... That kind of recipe for me in the past has kind of worked, and I've been fortunate to win two in a row.

"We need to be laser focused on ourselves. We need to take the lessons from that [Western Conference finals] series, for sure, and we did. But it's certainly not something that we overcorrect for, because you end up chasing your shadow, and it prevents you from being your best as you move forward."

ESPN's Summer Forecast gave Gilgeous-Alexander the fourth-best chance at the 2027 MVP, behind Victor Wembanyama, Nikola Jokic and Luka Doncic. No player has won three consecutive MVPs since Larry Bird in 1984, 1985 and 1986. -- Baxter Holmes

Doncic talks LeBron exit, Lakers "championship" ceiling
Speaking to ESPN's Brian Windhorst during Los Angeles Lakers media day, guard Luka Doncic detailed his reaction to LeBron James leaving for the Philadelphia 76ers this past summer and why he thinks a successful 2026-27 includes a Lakers run to the title:

"It was kind of sad. Playing with LeBron was amazing. There's a lot of things I learned from him. ... We all know who LeBron James is."

Shams: Duren's relationship with Pistons "has fractures"

Simmons "didn't touch a ball for a year"

During Sacramento Kings media day, guard Ben Simmons laid out the reasons he chose the Kings and why he's excited for the 2026-27 season.

"The expectations are low. I feel like that's been something on me too, so we can relate in that way," Simmons told reporters. "I think we have a chip on our shoulder."

Simmons last played in 2024-25, appearing in 51 games for the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers. The three-time All-Star said the time away gave him the chance to focus on "getting my body right and my mind right."

Pistons GM hasn't spoken with Duren all summer

Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons have a decision to make as the clock ticks closer to Oct. 1 -- the deadline to sign a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer.

For Duren, he can accept the five-year, $200 million contract that has been offered by Detroit or he can become the first player named All-NBA or All-Star to sign the qualifying offer. If he chooses the latter, Duren will hold veto power on any trade this season and be an unrestricted free agent next summer.

For the Pistons, weighing the risk of having an All-NBA player on a one-year contract and, more importantly, the likelihood he will depart next summer as a free agent is key.

There are eight projected teams that have significant cap space to sign Duren to a four-year, $189 million max contract.

"I can't control the different things that he does or his group does," Pistons president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon said at media day. "For me, it's control what we can and letting him know he is a big part of what we do."

Langdon also said he hasn't spoken with Duren all summer during Pistons media day. -- Bobby Marks

Mitchell: LeBron to Cavs made sense "for a lot of reasons"

At Cavaliers media day, Donovan Mitchell said that in his mind, he thought LeBron James would return to Cleveland because "for a lot of reasons it made sense."

"I didn't think Philly. I thought if he didn't come here, it'd be Golden State," Mitchell said.

After being swept in the Eastern Conference finals by the eventual champion New York Knicks then missing out on James in free agency, Cleveland kept its core intact. The Cavs signed Mitchell to a four-year, $273 million maximum extension and re-signed James Harden to a three-year, $97 million contract. Cleveland did make one major addition by acquiring Peyton Watson from the Denver Nuggets in a multiteam trade then signing the restricted free agent to a four-year, $88 million deal.

Speaking for the first time since their extensions, Mitchell and Harden both said their approaches to their new deals -- Mitchell signing as soon as he was eligible with Harden opting out to give Cleveland more flexibility to make moves -- reflected a team-first mindset.

"This is something that I want to do, and I want to win a championship," Harden said. "So, what does that look like? Making the team better, making the team whole to where we give ourselves a chance. By the way, you can have the best talented team, which I've been on before, and still not win.

"We waited, waited, waited until the front office called me, made sure that we got everything that we can get, and then we signed. We got a long way to go, but I love the direction and steps that we're taking here as a unit from top to bottom." -- Daniel Oyefusi

MacMahon: Thunder adjusting to roster changes
The departures of three championship-winning teammates doesn't yet feel like reality for Thunder superstar Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who kidded that he still expected Luguentz Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins to show up for Oklahoma City's team picture Monday afternoon.

"It's the business of the NBA, right?" Gilgeous-Alexander said, referring to the series of financially motivated trades. "I don't think anybody has played with all 12 guys their whole career. It sucks a little bit.

"My mind never even went to what we were going to be like on the court. It was more like the brotherhood."

As fellow OKC guard Jalen Williams added, "It's the weirdest thing ever." -- Tim MacMahon

Clippers announce Ingram has partially torn Achilles

The LA Clippers announced they found a partially torn Achilles tendon in Brandon Ingram's foot after his recent heel surgery. He will miss the start of the 2026-27 season.

Jokic: "I'm gonna sign next year"

Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic reiterated his commitment to the franchise at Monday's media day.

"I'm gonna sign next year," Jokic said. "If they want me."

Curry said knee is ready to go for the season

Golden State Warriors superstar guard Stephen Curry addressed the media Monday in offering positive updates on his injured knee.

"Knee's feeling great. Ready to go. No issues," Curry said. "I feel a lot stronger and understanding of what I'm dealing with."

Curry did acknowledge a "management element" but said there are currently no restrictions.

Nuggets confident in Jokic's future with franchise

Members of the Denver Nuggets' front office, general manager Jon Wallace and executive vice president of basketball Ben Tenzer addressed the media on Monday and answered questions regarding Nikola Jokic's future with the franchise. The three-time MVP didn't sign an extension this offseason.

"We feel very comfortable with the relation and trust there," Tenzer said. "We have no concerns."

LeBron: I wanted to finish my career with the Knicks
New Philadelphia 76er LeBron James said his decision came down to five teams this offseason and that he envisioned going to the New York Knicks before they won the 2026 title.

"I had visions of playing in [Madison Square] Garden and finishing my career in the Garden," James told ESPN on Monday during the 76ers' media day. "One of the best places I've ever played.

"I think it's the No. 1 arena in the world, as far as for a basketball player. But after they beat San Antonio, I was like, 'Hey, I can't.' I couldn't do it."

James and the 76ers will play the Knicks at the Garden on opening night, Oct. 20.

No update on Gary Trent Jr. investigation

Milwaukee Bucks governor Wes Edens did not provide an update on the league investigation into Gary Trent Jr.'s contract.

"I don't have any update," Edens said. "We're working with the league and fully cooperating with them. But I don't have any insight beyond that."

The NBA is looking into a potential cap-circumvention violation by the Bucks around Trent's deal this offseason.

Cronin: Blazers have "belief" in Ja Morant
Portland Trail Blazers' general manager Joe Cronin addressed why the franchise decided to trade for Ja Morant this offseason during Portland's media day on Monday.

"Just straight belief in Ja," Cronin said. "Our view of Ja as still a very high-level player.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit, but we're very focused on talent."

Cronin also said veteran guard Jrue Holiday could play some minutes on the wing for Portland this season, while adding that Holiday and veteran guard Damian Lillard will have a positive influence on Morant.

Kerr: Rookie Lendeborg going to "play a ton"

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said during Monday's media day that he expects rookie Yaxel Lendeborg to "play a ton" this season.

"He's clearly going to play a ton," Kerr said. "He gives us the size and the versatility that we need.

"Whether he's a starter or coming off the bench, that will be determined the next couple of weeks."

Lendeborg was the No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft and averaged 15.1 points per game at Michigan last season.

Embiid: 'Extremely excited' about this year's team
Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid said Monday that he feels like the team finally has the right mix of players, after an offseason in which the franchise traded for Jaylen Brown and signed LeBron James to join the young guard tandem of VJ Edgecombe and Tyrese Maxey.

"It's hard to win when you get a group of guys together for one year, two years, maybe," he said. "I'm extremely excited about this team because we have the right mix of veteran leadership and younger guys. We might have some ups and downs, but we're gonna get there."

Wembanyama addresses last year's Finals loss
After leading by double digits in each of the five games in last season's NBA Finals, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama said his memories of it will fuel the team this season.

"I couldn't imagine a better motivation," he said.

Harper addresses role for coming season
After offseason chatter about his role, San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper said he'd follow the coaches' lead this season.

"Everyone has a competitive edge to them. But the biggest thing for me is whatever I can do, just like last year, to help the team win," he said. "Whatever position the coaches think is best for me to be in, that's the position I'll happily go in."

First look at LeBron in a 76ers uniform
New Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James is taking questions from reporters on Monday. Here's what he had to say when asked about his initial impressions of his team:

"Everybody is on the same page," James said. "We are all speaking the same language."

LeBron addressed his role too, saying he's open to whatever the team needs from him to win.

"Whatever they need me to do," he said. "The luxury of my game is I can do everything. ... Literally, I can do everything"

Kawhi: I was a distraction, ready to move forward
In his first public appearance with the Toronto Raptors after a controversy-filled summer, Kawhi Leonard addressed the NBA's investigation into him and his business dealings.

"I know why some of you guys came. You want to hear about the investigation. But in talking with the NBA and PA, I think the best decision is to move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor," he said. "I already was a distraction for the past 70 days and wasn't able to meet my teammates or do any of that stuff, minicamp stuff, so, moving forward, I just want to talk about the Toronto Raptors."

Haliburton: I am 100% healthy
Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton said Monday that he is healthy and ready for the season.

"I am healthy. I am 100%," he said. "There will be no restrictions. That is not news. There is no source. I am the source. I am ready to go for the year."

Porzingis out indefinitely in blow to Warriors
Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis is out indefinitely to open training camp with a health issue, according to the team.
In late July, Porzingis agreed to a two-year, $40 million contract with a player option on the second season to return to the Warriors.

Brown: KAT, Hart extension talks won't be a distraction
After reports surfaced last week that negotiations between the New York Knicks and center Karl-Anthony Towns had hit a stalemate, coach Mike Brown said Monday neither Towns' situation nor Hart's would linger in the locker room.

"We talk about everything [with the team]," Brown said. "We don't want to have any elephants in the room."

"I'm not involved in it. They'll figure it out. Control what you can control."

And here's what Towns said about a potential extension: "I've made it known I want to play here. Been a fan since I was a kid. I'd like to get it done."

Hornets GM: Brandon Miller to be ready for training camp
After undergoing offseason surgery on his left shoulder, Hornets wing Brandon Miller should be a full participant in training camp and "ready to roll" for opening night, Hornets general manager Jeff Peterson said Monday.

Miller, 23, is entering his fourth NBA season after being the No. 2 pick in the 2023 draft.

Duren won't be at Pistons media day, start of camp
Detroit Pistons All-Star center Jalen Duren is not attending the team's media day on Monday or the start of training camp as his contract standoff continues, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Monday.

Duren, a restricted free agent, is declining the team's five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed offer as both sides remain at a stalemate ahead of the Thursday deadline on a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer, sources said.

Sept. 26

Bulls trade Dillingham to Hornets for Hield, cash
The Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets agreed to a trade sending Rob Dillingham to Charlotte for Buddy Hield and cash, the teams announced Saturday.

2026 NBA offseason trade grades

Sept. 25

What's next for Curry and the Warriors?
Stephen Curry's two-year, $116 million extension made him the first player in NBA history to amass $600 million in career on-court earnings.

The deal has also put the Golden State Warriors in position to have extra spending power next summer.

By Curry taking $10 million less than the maximum allowed, the Warriors project to have nearly $38 million in cap space in 2027. Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million.

For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. They will be free agents next summer.

Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski. The 2023 first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks

Grading the Curry deal: Why Warriors don't get an A

Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury
The Charlotte Hornets announced that Kon Knueppel will be out for at least the entire preseason because of a left hamstring injury.

James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers
LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July.

"[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump."

Grizzlies waive Russell
The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.
